PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: October 1, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026265 Can internship experiences bridge the gap between university training and work readiness? Evidence from vietnamese economics students Vi Truong Thi Thuya | Duong Pham Ngoca aUniversity of Finance – Marketing, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Abstract This study investigates the influence of business internship experiences on the work readiness of economics students in Vietnam, addressing a critical gap in the country’s higher education-employment linkage. Grounded in the Knowledge–Skills–Abilities (KSA) framework and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the study examines how professional skills and work motivation serve as dual mediators in the relationship between internship participation and students’ readiness for the labor market. A structured survey was conducted with 389 final-year economics students from four major universities in Ho Chi Minh City. Structural equation modeling using SmartPLS 4.0 was applied to test the proposed model. The findings demonstrate that internships have both direct and indirect effects on work readiness. Specifically, internships significantly enhance professional skills, which in turn foster greater intrinsic motivation, leading to improved work readiness. Among the mediators, professional skills emerged as the stronger factor, while work motivation acted as an amplifier of the internship’s effect. The study provides empirical evidence that supports integrating practical experience into academic programs, particularly in emerging economies where theoretical training often dominates. Practical recommendations are offered for universities to develop structured and skill-oriented internship programs, for businesses to play a proactive role in student development, and for policymakers to align internship policies with national workforce strategies. This research not only contributes to the literature on graduate employability but also delivers actionable insights for stakeholders aiming to close the gap between academic training and labor market demands in Vietnam and similar contexts. Keywords: internship, work readiness, professional skills, work motivation, vietnam higher education 1. Introduction In the context of current socio-economic development, the quality of human resources is considered a decisive factor in the competitiveness of each country. In particular, the group of young workers and university graduates play an important role in supplementing high-quality human resources for the labor market. The willingness of graduates to work not only reflects the training quality of higher education institutions but also directly affects their entry into the labor market, improves labor productivity, and promotes sustainable economic development (Manh, 2023; Nam, 2022). In Vietnam, according to a report by the Ministry of Education and Training, the rate of students having jobs after 12 months of graduation is 98%, and some universities even announced this rate as high as 100% (Manh, 2023). However, in addition to the positive figures, in reality, many graduates do not participate in the labor market or work in unrelated fields, leading to a waste of social resources and reduced efficiency in educational investment (Ly, 2024; Nam, 2022). The main reason comes from the lack of connection between university training and the actual needs of the labor market, as well as the limitations in career orientation of students right from the beginning (Nghiem & Cuong, 2022). A notable shortcoming is that training programs in higher education institutions remain heavily theoretical and lack alignment with current market needs. The training process has not really met the expectations of businesses, causing graduates to lack confidence and practical skills to be ready to work immediately (Ristiani & Farah, 2022; Sari & Rahdiyanta, 2023). Meanwhile, when choosing a major, students lack information about labor market trends and demands, leading to misaligned academic pursuits and unclear career plans (Ly, 2024). To overcome the above limitations, the Government issued Decree No. 73/2015/ND-CP on standards, stratification and ranking of higher education institutions, along with Circular No. 17/2021/TT-BGDDT regulating training program standards. Accordingly, universities are required to adjust their training programs towards enhancing professional practice, in which the business internship module becomes mandatory, accounting for 6-8 credits, equivalent to 10 weeks of practical internship at enterprises (Circular No. 17/2021/TT-BGDĐT, 2021). (2023) In Vietnam, studies on the impact of business internship on students' readiness to work are still limited. The work of Nghiem & Cuong (2022) only stopped at identifying personal factors such as social intelligence, psychological capital, and sense of connection, but did not fully consider the role of business internships. Meanwhile, the implementation of business internships in universities faces many challenges such as internship content not being close to the major, lack of close coordination between schools and businesses, or students are only assigned simple tasks that have no practical learning value (Hong & Huong, 2022). This research gap is especially evident in the economic sector, where students need practical experience to develop skills as well as soft skills to meet the strict requirements of the labor market. International studies such as those of Fauzan et al. (2023), Hanifah et al. (2023), and Shaheen et al. (2022) both confirmed the important mediating role of professional skills and work motivation in the relationship between business internship and students' work readiness. These results show that, for business internship to be truly effective, there needs to be a synchronous combination between training programs, internship content, and support mechanisms from enterprises. To address these gaps, the objective of this study is to examine the direct and indirect effects of business internships on students’ work readiness in Vietnam, with a specific focus on the mediating roles of professional skills and work motivation. By doing so, the study aims to provide empirical insights into how practical experience enhances employability outcomes in emerging economies. While internships are widely recognized for enhancing employability, the specific mechanisms through which they influence students’ work readiness, particularly via professional skills and intrinsic motivation, remain underexplored in the Vietnamese higher education context. To fill this gap, the study uses a combination of the Knowledge–Skills–Abilities (KSA) framework and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), applying it to the analysis of the effect of business internships on students’ work readiness. The study focuses on the two mediating components of professional skills and work motivation. If this dual mediation is proven empirically, it will provide novel insights into bridging academic learning and employability in countries with economies in transition, such as Vietnam. 2. Theoretical Foundation and Research Hypotheses 2.1. Theoretical Foundation of Work Readiness Work readiness is the full level of preparation of an individual to participate effectively in the real working environment (Caballero et al., 2011). From the view of career psychology, the Career Adaptability Theory (CAT) by Savickas (2005) says that the shift from school to business place demands on individuals to develop core competencies for example: concern, control, curiosity, and confidence. These factors help students adapt better to changes and challenges from the working environment. At the same time, the KSA model (Knowledge, Skills, Attitudes) of McClelland (1973) emphasizes that work readiness is formed on the basis of knowledge, skills and work attitudes. In particular, skills and attitudes are two elements that can only be truly developed through practical experiences such as business internships (BI). The Work Readiness Scale (Caballero et al., 2011) also reinforces this argument by pointing out that communication skills, understanding of corporate culture, confidence and adaptability are important to work readiness. The above arguments affirm that BI experience is the bridge. It helps students strengthen their adaptability, develop skills and professional attitudes— thereby improving the level of work readiness upon graduation. Fugate et al. (2004) provided the theoretical underpinning for career adaptability which is very proximal to work readiness; it highlights an individual's capacity to deal with changes and challenges that have to be coped with in the job domain and thus is an important conceptual basis for understanding how students move into the job market. 2.2. The Role of Business Internships in Work Readiness BI is one of the crucial factors that link classroom theory with professional practice. As stated by Coll & Zegwaard (2006), business internship equips students to apply their knowledge in the business setting, hence clarifying the relationship between career requirements and actual work contexts. Also, according to Narayanan et al. (2010), business internship inspires students to develop problem-solving skills, critical thinking, and teamwork; talents without which the school-to-business undertaking would be impossible. It is within the internship that practical contexts help reinforce what was learned theoretically from classroom lectures. According to the words of Cicilia et al. (2023), it is through effective mentorship that students can bridge academic lessons with https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Thuy and Ngoc (2026) 3 actual work practices. This, therefore, reinstates the need for structured internship programs in as far as enhancing student readiness for work is concerned. Internships are the critical bridge that goes beyond skill acquisition, connecting academic learning with workplace readiness. The experience of being an intern enables students to learn how to apply their theoretical lessons in the practical context of professional environments (Syafira & Umam, 2023; Usman & Choirunnisa, 2020). More importantly, internship participation places the student in a better position with enhanced work motivation. According to the Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000), engaging real-world work tasks fulfills the basic psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness that underlie intrinsic motivation. Empirical studies show that meaningful internships help students clarify their professional goals and enhance their self-awareness (Syafira & Umam, 2023; Usman & Choirunnisa, 2020). In Vietnam, research by (Oanh et al., 2021) showed that students participating in business internship have significantly improved their professional skills, especially in fields requiring high practicality such as economics and management. However, the quality of business internship is still limited due to the lack of close coordination between schools and businesses, and the internship content is not close to the training major (Hong & Huong, 2022). From the above theoretical and practical bases, the study proposes: H1: Business internships have a positive impact on students' professional skills. H2: Business internships have a positive impact on students' work motivation. 2.3. Mechanism of Impact of Professional Skills on Motivation and Readiness to Work Professional skills are not only a tool to help students perform well in their work tasks but also a key factor affecting work motivation and readiness to enter the labor market. According to the Job Characteristics Model (Hackman & Oldham, 1976), when individuals possess solid skills, they will feel the meaning of their work, thereby increasing satisfaction and intrinsic motivation. Empirical studies have clarified this relationship. Judge et al. (2001) affirmed that professional skills are a mediating factor that helps transform the impact of environmental factors (such as BI) into sustainable work motivation. Syafira & Umam (2023) also showed that students with good professional skills often have higher work motivation due to self-confidence and a clear sense of self-worth. In addition, professional skills also have a direct impact on work readiness. Fauzan et al. (2023) and Hanifah et al. (2023) both pointed out that students with good professional skills are able to adapt faster to the working environment, thereby improving their work readiness. Research by Shore & Dinning (2023) shows that students with developed professional skills easily transition from the learning environment to the formal working environment with higher efficiency. In Vietnam, research by Trang et al. (2022) affirms that professional skills are an important factor in helping economics students improve their work readiness in the context of a competitive labor market. Based on these theoretical and empirical foundations, the study proposes: H3: Professional skills have a positive impact on students' work motivation. H4: Professional skills have a positive impact on students' work readiness. 2.4. Mechanism of work motivation on work readiness Work motivation is an intrinsic psychological factor that helps students maintain efforts, overcome challenges and proactively participate in the labor market (Ryan & Deci, 2000). When motivation is activated by awareness of career values and self-efficacy, students will tend to proactively seek job opportunities, thereby increasing their work readiness (Fugate et al., 2004). Van Der Heijde & Van Der Heijden (2006) also pointed out that high work motivation helps students have a positive attitude in the job search process, increasing their ability to adapt to the new environment. Hanifah et al. (2023) and Fauzan et al. (2023) asserted that work motivation is a key mediating factor that helps transform the impact of business internship experience and career skills into actual work readiness. In the context of graduate employability, Feriady & Yanto (2018) conducted an empirical study to identify the key components of students' work readiness. The results they obtained indicated for us the importance of psychological preparedness, professional competences, adherence to organizational norms, and the capacity to manage and deal with challenges at the workplace as critical determinants of work readiness. These critical insights were to a large extent embraced in further research and, therefore, taken as key guiding principles in developing the measurement scales for work readiness in this study. In Vietnam, according to the study by Nuong's (2024), it is the students with a strong motivation towards work who show a greater pro-activeness in the accumulation of experience, in the practice of skills, and shows a higher level of work readiness when entering the labor market. Therefore, the study proposes the following hypothesis: H5: Work motivation has a positive impact on students' work readiness. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Thuy and Ngoc (2026) 4 2.5. Research model and proposed hypothesis Drawing on the theoretical frameworks of CAT, KSA, and Self-Determination Theory, alongside empirical evidence, this study constructs a model to examine the influence of business internships (BI) on students’ work readiness through two mediating mechanisms: professional skills and work motivation. Business internships serve as the initiating factor, fostering the development of professional skills and enhancing work motivation. Professional skills exert both direct and indirect effects (via motivation) on work readiness. Work motivation, as a critical psychological intermediary, facilitates the transformation of the impacts from skills and business internships into tangible work readiness. This model emphasizes the indirect relationship between the business internship and work readiness, assumed to have been in addition to the direct impacts, through two intermediary variables. It has been well documented in many previous studies, such as Fauzan et al. (2023), Hanifah et al. (2023), and Shaheen et al. (2022) that the impact of business internship on work readiness is believed to be in the main through developing professional skills and stimulating students' work motivation.. In Vietnam, studies such as Trang et al. (2022) also support this argument when pointing out that BI affects work readiness through improving skills and attitudes, while work motivation is the core factor that helps students transform values from internship experiences into labor market readiness behavior (Figure 1). From there, the study proposes the following hypothesis: H6: Business internships have an indirect impact on students' work readiness through skills and work motivation. Figure 1 Proposed research model. Research hypotheses: H1: Business internship has a positive impact on students' career skills. H2: Business internship has a positive impact on students' work motivation. H3: Career skills have a positive impact on students' work motivation. H4: Career skills have a positive impact on students' work readiness. H5: Work motivation has a positive impact on students' work readiness. H6: Business internship has an indirect impact on students' work readiness through career skills and work motivation. 3. Materials and Methods 3.1. Characteristics of the research sample and data collection method The study surveyed economics students in Ho Chi Minh City to examine the role of business internships (BI) in their work readiness (WR). The survey will focus on final-year students or those who have graduated recently, and who completed their business internships not more than 12 months prior to this survey; this timing will help maintain the context of the research and the dynamics of the process of preparing to enter the labor market. For representativeness, a stratified random sampling method was used. The approach divides the population into similar subgroups or strata from which samples are then randomly selected to be proportionally represented (Creswell & Poth, 2023). The strata for this study are the universities the students in the economics program belonged to, with the population based in Ho Chi Minh City and four major institutions: University of Finance – Marketing (UFM), Ho Chi Minh University of Banking (HUB), University of Economics and Law (UEL), and University of Economics and Finance (UEF). These universities were chosen because they offer majors in economics and have large student populations. The proportionate sample size per stratum was based on the estimated number of final-year economics students at each university, as outlined in the guidelines for stratified https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Thuy and Ngoc (2026) 5 sampling to make the approach more representative (Saunders et al., 2023). From there, random sampling within each stratum was done to select participants, making sure the choice of the target population was unbiased. Data were collected through an online survey questionnaire, using Google Forms to make sure flexibility and access was optimized. In supporting the content of this paper, we worked with instructors and academic advisors at the universities to which our students belonged, ensuring the right students would take part in the survey. A total of 389 valid questionnaires were returned. The sample distribution is presented in Table 1, which shows the proportional representation of each university. Table 1 Demographic Profiles. Scale and measurement of research variables Concepts of research are measured on a 5-level Likert scale, from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The variable scales have previously been used and were modified to fit the Vietnamese context of the research. The business Internship variable is borrowed from Narayanan et al. (2010), and it includes the Practical participation level, Relevance of content, support from businesses, and proactive learning on the part of the students. The Professional skills variable adopts the scale of Gault et al. (2000) and Van Der Heijde & Van Der Heijden (2006), which includes problem-solving ability, communication skills, group work, adaptation into businesses, time management, and self-study The Work Motivation variable is based on the scale of Gagné et al. (2015) and Ryan & Deci (2000), and it comprises intrinsic motivation and perceived values of the career, growth expectations, initiative, and engagement Finally, the Work Readiness variable inherits Caballero et al. (2011), in terms of confidence level, adaptability, and knowledge-skills preparation, proactive attitude and awareness of professional responsibility. The questionnaire was pilot-tested with 30 students to ensure clarity, comprehension, and alignment with Vietnam’s cultural-educational context. 3.3. Data analysis After collection, the data will be processed and analyzed by statistical software SPSS and SmartPLS 4.0. First of all, the data will be checked preliminarily to see whether the questionnaires are invalid or not, and the reliability of the scale will be tested through Cronbach’s Alpha and Composite Reliability(CR). The value of Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient is 0.7, is considered acceptable reliability (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994). Then factor loading, AVE index and Fornell-Larcker criteria would be used to check convergent and discriminant validity of the scales. Values >0.7 and >0.5 are considered convergent validity (Hair et al., 2019). The research model and hypotheses will be tested using structural equation modeling (SEM-PLS), applicable for data of mean sample size and models with mediating factors. Measures of the goodness-of-fit used will be R², f², and Q². with the dependent variable, along with the explained variance of the dependent variable, and f² as individual impact measures, and Q² as a predictive ability measure. To examine the mediating effects of professional skills and work motivation on the relationship between BI and work readiness, the study applies the Bootstrap method along with confidence interval testing using 5,000 replicate samples as suggested by Hayes (2013). The analysis results will allow determining the direct and indirect influence of factors in the model, thereby clarifying the overall impact mechanism. 3.4. Discussion This study confirmed the significant impact of business internships (BI) on students' work readiness (WR), both directly and indirectly through professional skills (PS) and work motivation (WM). The validated relationships within the proposed model demonstrate strong empirical consistency, aligning with the underlying theoretical frameworks. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Thuy and Ngoc (2026) 9 The direct influence of BI on PS proved to be very strong, supporting the role of internships as a vital bridge between academic knowledge and practical competencies. This finding corresponds with what has been found in prior research by Shore & Dinning (2023) and Syafira et al. (2023) who found that internships presented an excellent avenue through which theoretical learning could be converted into vital workplace skills like communication, problem-solving, and adaptability. The study also revealed a major impact of BI on WM. It proved that internships do not only result in skill development but also spark intrinsic motivation that leads to the creation of a positive aptitude for self-determination and interest in a vocation. This finding is in line with the viewpoint of the Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000) and is as well supported by the empirical evidence of Usman & Choirunnisa (2020). They proved that meaningful internship experiences raise students' perceptions regarding career values and lead to the encouragement of proactive engagement. The link between PS and WM was further established, showing that enhanced career competencies make for clearer motivation and clearer professional aspirations. This result is in line with the Career Adaptability model (Fugate et al., 2004) and with which Fauzan et al. (2023) and Hanifah et al. (2023) had also noted the foundational role of professional skills in building students’ motivation and career orientation. Both PS and WM showed significant impacts on WR; therefore, the students’ readiness results from the synthesis of the practical skills and psychological factors. This is in line with the argument of Usman & Choirunnisa and also Fauzan et al. that intrinsic motivational factors in addition to competence factors shape work readiness, not just the academic readiness itself. The study clarified the indirect pathways through which BI enhances WR. The indirect effect through PS was strongest next to it, followed by WM and the combined chain BI → PS → WM → WR. This multi-step mechanism underscores the strategic importance of internships in fostering long-term employability, beyond immediate experiential gains. Such detailed insights make up a key contribution of this study, setting it apart from research precedent in Vietnam, where the mediating roles of PS and WM were not fully probed (Nghiem & Cuong, 2022). Also, the WM appearing as a mediating factor speaks the context specific nature of the higher education system in Vietnam, which is still heavily theory-driven with no structured practical training. In this setting, internships emerge as the most important intervention, bridging skills gaps while making students become self-driven toward career readiness. This gives a very important view, supplementing the international findings with real evidence from a less researched emerging economy (Shaheen et al., 2022). This study improves the explanation of how business internships develop work readiness among students, using empirical evidence to support the dual intervening mechanisms of professional skills and work motivation. The Knowledge– Skills–Abilities (KSA) model is merged with Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to fully explain the relationship between the two variables, internship and employability, offering valuable novelty that could be applied in real terms in the Vietnamese context and also fill relevant gaps in the literature. The dual-pathway model enriches the existing theories by considering skill acquisition and motivational improvement together, two aspects that have hitherto been examined in the literature as single paradigms. 6. Conclusions This study examines how business internships enhance students’ work readiness. It elaborates on the mediation effect of professional skills and work motivation. From an empirical study, it was confirmed that the internships equips students with significant practical competencies while fostering their intrinsic motivation, which is directly related to finding a job. By explaining this dual pathway mechanism, the current study creates a full understanding of how internships actually make an academic student ready for work in the real world, especially in countries like Vietnam. It thus adds value to existing literature on graduate employability by offering a direct, implementable prescription for making internship programs in the higher education setting more effective. 6.1. Contribution of the study Prior studies focused on direct effects while this research emphasizes the dual mediation of skills and motivation; together, they offer a more comprehensive understanding of how internships actually foster work readiness. Prior studies have not sufficiently explained the direct effects between the internship experiences and outcomes in employment; rather, they have mostly examined direct effects or single mediating variables. The present research integrates the KSA framework and Self-Determination Theory for a more comprehensive explanation of the translation of internship experiences into outcomes. Besides theoretical insights, the study provides practical implications for universities and businesses in designing internship programs that can develop student technical competencies along with building intrinsic motivation. The evidence is provided from Vietnam, a place with scarce former research on the topic, thereby adding valuable perspectives to the global discourse on graduate employability in emerging economies. 7. Managerial implications https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Thuy and Ngoc (2026) 10 The study empirically demonstrates the role of business internships in enhancing students’ work readiness by developing professional skills and work motivation. The findings not only reinforce theoretical arguments but also bring important practical implications for schools, businesses, and educational administrators. 7.1. For higher education institutions The research results confirm that BI is the factor with the strongest influence on students' work readiness. This poses an urgent requirement for universities to improve the quality of internship programs, transforming from “procedural form” to “substantive experience”. Specifically, schools need to: Build strategic links with businesses: Not only stop at signing cooperation agreements, but also need to deeply participate in the process of building internship content, ensuring that students have access to professional tasks in their field. Integrate practical skills training activities before and during the business internship process: Training courses on soft skills, professional attitudes, and corporate culture need to be implemented systematically so that students are fully prepared. Design an internship assessment mechanism associated with output standards: Assessment should not only be based on formal comments from businesses, but should have specific criteria reflecting the progress in skills, awareness and career motivation of students. Research shows that developing skills not only helps students be more ready to work, but also directly promotes work motivation, thereby creating a double effect in the transition from school to the labor market. 7.2. For businesses Businesses are the central factor in the process of students developing skills and career motivation from internships. Research results confirm that business internship is only effective when students are assigned practical tasks and participate in real working environments. Therefore, businesses need to: Shift from “supporter” to “direct trainer” role: Businesses need to build internship programs with clear goals, methodical training plans and assign appropriate instructors, considering interns as part of the process of developing future human resources. Increase opportunities to experience real career tasks: Instead of assigning simple administrative tasks, businesses should create conditions for students to participate in projects and professional work groups to develop skills and career thinking. Establish a mechanism to record contributions and provide regular feedback: This not only helps students increase their motivation to work but also increases the ability to recruit potential candidates after graduation. The study confirms that support from businesses is the factor that "activates" the development of students' capacity and readiness to work. 7.3. For policy makers The research results have shown the gap between the training goals of schools and the actual needs of the labor market. Therefore, promoting cooperation mechanisms between schools and businesses needs to be placed in the national human resource development strategy. Education managers need to: Clearly define output standards on skills and work readiness for each industry group. Issue policies to encourage enterprises to participate deeply in the internship training process: it can be tax incentives, the title of companion education enterprise, or support for the construction of internal training centers associated with universities. Monitor the quality of business internships as a criterion for assessing the quality of higher education: This helps ensure that internships are not just a formal requirement but are actually a bridge to help students integrate into the labor market. This study shows that Business internship is not just a supplementary course but a core factor determining the output quality of young human resources. Integrating internships into national human resource strategies is no longer optional but essential for ensuring graduates’ readiness to meet dynamic labor market demands. 8. Limitations and future research directions This study employed a stratified sampling approach to ensure representativeness across key student groups, enhancing the reliability of the findings within the targeted population. However, certain limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample was limited to economics students from selected Vietnamese universities. While the stratified sampling method helped capture diversity within this group, the findings may not fully generalize to students in other academic disciplines, such as engineering, health sciences, or education, where internship experiences and employability dynamics may differ. Future research is recommended to extend the model to a broader range of disciplines and institutional contexts to validate the applicability of these results. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Thuy and Ngoc (2026) 11 Second, the study was conducted within a specific geographical and educational context, reflecting the characteristics of the Vietnamese higher education system. Cross-regional and cross-country comparative studies could offer insights into how contextual factors shape the link between internships and employability in emerging economies. Finally, this research employed a cross-sectional design, capturing perceptions at a single point in time. Longitudinal studies are suggested to examine the long-term effects of internship experiences on graduates’ career development and employability outcomes. Additionally, future research could explore moderating variables such as gender, academic performance, or organizational support to further elucidate the mechanisms through which internships enhance work readiness. Informed consent was obtained online, and participation was voluntary, anonymous, and without risk. No personal identifiers were collected. JSON: Name: internship_work_readiness_vn_pls_sem Title: Partial least squares structural equation modeling of the effects of business internship participation on economics students' work readiness in Vietnam Short Hypothesis: Participation in structured business internships increases economics students' work readiness via improvements in professional skills and intrinsic work motivation. Related Work: Existing empirical work has measured internship effects on graduate employability using survey-based correlational designs and structural models. Prior approaches typically estimate direct effects of internship participation on employability or include a single mediator such as soft skills or motivation. Measurement strategies vary across studies, ranging from bespoke scales to validated multidimensional instruments, and estimation techniques include covariance-based SEM and PLS-SEM. Key limitations in current work are: reliance on cross-sectional self-report data susceptible to common-method bias; narrow focus on single mediators, which obscures potential joint mediation chains; limited geographic or disciplinary scope reducing external validity; inconsistent reporting of measurement validity and predictive checks; and infrequent robustness comparisons between PLS-SEM and alternative estimators. Few studies evaluate effect sizes, predictive ability, or conduct ablation/multigroup analyses to test model stability across institutions or student subgroups. Abstract: This research evaluates whether business internship participation increases work readiness among final-year economics students in Vietnam and investigates dual mediation by professional skills and intrinsic work motivation. Using a structured survey of university students and a latent-variable modeling approach, the study operationalizes internship exposure, professional skills, work motivation, and work readiness with validated multidimensional scales and estimates direct and indirect pathways via partial least squares structural equation modeling. The primary contribution is an empirical decomposition of internship effects into skill-based and motivation-based channels, quantifying relative effect sizes and predictive power. Expected outcomes include (1) evidence that internships exert both direct and mediated influences on readiness, (2) quantification of the stronger mediator between skills and motivation, and (3) model-level predictive diagnostics to inform program design. Findings aim to inform university curricula, employer internship design, and policy measures to improve graduate employability in emerging-economy contexts. Experiments: Dataset: primary cross-sectional survey of final-year or recently graduated economics students from at least four universities in Ho Chi Minh City; target N>=400; record university, gender, GPA, internship duration, internship type, and time since internship. Measurement: constructs BI (business internship exposure: 7 items), PS (professional skills: 6 items), WM (work motivation: 4 items), WR (work readiness: 6 items) on 5-point Likert scales; include one unrelated marker variable for common-method bias tests. Baselines: (A) direct-effect model (BI -> WR); (B) single-mediator models (BI -> PS -> WR) and (BI -> WM -> WR); (C) dual-mediator model (BI -> PS, BI -> WM, PS -> WM, PS -> WR, WM -> WR) as primary model; (D) reverse-causality model (WR -> BI) for directionality check. Estimators: primary estimation with PLS-SEM (SmartPLS or equivalent), robustness checks using covariance-based SEM (MLR) and OLS path regressions. Validation and fit: report outer loadings, Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, HTMT, VIF; report R2, f2, Q2 (PLSpredict), standardized path coefficients, t-values, p-values from bootstrapping (5,000 samples), and RMSEpredict. Hypothesis tests: bootstrap indirect effect estimates with 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals for mediation; compare indirect effect magnitudes. Ablation study: compare full dual-mediator model to models with PS removed and WM removed; report changes in total effect, indirect effect, R2(WR), and f2 for omitted paths. Subgroup analyses: multi-group PLS by university and by internship duration (>=10 weeks vs <10 weeks) with permutation tests for path invariance. Robustness checks: Harman single-factor test and marker-variable method for common-method variance; sensitivity analysis of results to removal of top/bottom 5% response times and to alternative scale codings. Preprocessing: handle missing data with multiple imputation if missing-at-random and exclude cases with >25% item nonresponse; standardize indicators for CB-SEM. Reporting: present full path diagram, standardized coefficients, indirect effect decomposition, and PLSpredict out-of-sample performance. Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional self-report design limits causal inference and is vulnerable to common-method and social-desirability bias. Sample restricted to economics students in one city reduces external validity across disciplines and regions. Measurement risk: item wording or cultural adaptation may reduce construct validity; single-language instruments may not capture nuance. Model risk: omitted variable bias (unmeasured factors like prior work experience or socio-economic status) can confound estimated paths; multicollinearity between mediators may inflate variance and obscure individual mediator effects. Statistical power: subgroup and multigroup tests require larger N; underpowered samples yield unstable bootstrap intervals. PLS-SEM limitations: lack of global fit indices comparable to CB-SEM can complicate model assessment; results may differ under alternative estimators. Data quality risks: nonresponse bias and inaccurate recall about internship content/duration. Generalization limits: findings may not hold for other fields, countries, or internship formats (virtual, micro-internships). Computationally, large bootstrap and multigroup procedures increase runtime but remain tractable on standard research hardware.
